inline.s: Adapting to change — this is hard to put into words. No one but takes the pursuit of gain and the avoidance of harm as the natural way of things, yet I do not. There are also cases where gain and harm are set before one and cannot be turned aside: that is change. How then is one to penetrate it? The multitude follow it; the noble person examines it; the sage accords with it. According with it, he does not possess it. Because he does not make it his own, therefore it is not his.

People call one who steals things a thief; he is not the thief. I call one who steals the mind a thief. How true this is! Now the stealer of things: he does not necessarily take all; where there is a guard he surely cannot enter; if he enters he is surely caught; caught, he dies without pardon. Since he dies, what has he stolen? But the stealer of the mind: he loses it utterly; the more urgently you guard, the deeper he enters; if caught, he lives, and often he is let go, and there are even those who teach him. Be on your guard!

The Way flourishes in yielding; virtue flourishes in humility; things break when they reach their full. Hence the yielding grows ever stronger, the humble ever brighter, the broken ever nearer to ruin. Those of old who did not make things their affair — they alone endured.

One who is meticulous in affairs is lax in mind; one who is meticulous in mind succeeds in affairs. Thus the more meticulous the affairs, the laxer the mind; the more meticulous the mind, the more successful the affairs. If the mind is not washed, there is no way to be meticulous. Therefore the sage values the washing of the mind and withdraws, hidden in secrecy.
A single thorn in the skin makes one toss and turn, ill at ease; a host of thorns in the mind — how can one be at ease? A thorn in the skin rots the skin; a thorn in the mind destroys the mind.

Great awe is to be feared. Look at the killing severity of heaven and earth: that is great awe. Though the myriad things be many, who can withstand their withering? Therefore one who possesses awe receives it from Heaven. Heaven’s awe is perfectly impartial; human awe imitates that impartiality. Heaven’s awe loves beings; human awe gives life.

To transform others earns no merit; to transform oneself earns merit. If one is truly transformed, others are transformed without being transformed. Witness how the countenance of a person of virtue makes a man’s contentiousness melt away. How true!

To deal with adversity is easy; to deal with prosperity is hard. Adversity has a counterpart; prosperity has none by which to know it. Therefore one who knows meets adversity as sweet dew and fears prosperity as poisoned wine — the utmost of care. Because of that care, his guard is never lost. Care — is it not the mark of one whose virtue is complete?

The substance of mind is originally bright; the dust of feeling thickens day by day. As the dust thickens, the mind grows daily dimmer. Therefore the sage uses wisdom and does not use feeling. So one who would reach the Way uses wisdom to remove feeling; when feeling is forgotten, wisdom too dissolves. One who forgets feeling is near the Way.

Wisdom is vast, affairs are slight. Nothing serves to penetrate affairs like wisdom. Thus the instrument of wisdom blunts the keen and unties the tangled, all to its advantage. Just watch a fleck of snow touch a red-hot furnace, or clear frost dissolve in the blazing sun: they are overcome. So one who overcomes himself — who can withstand him?

Others use great cleverness; I use the utmost simplicity. Cleverness loses by it; simplicity gains. Therefore one skilled in the Way casts away cleverness and takes simplicity, and nothing is not gained.

What accords with me delights me; what opposes me angers me. Delight and anger alternate; likes and dislikes contend. Day by day one’s faults increase. Tracing the cause to its root, it lies in not awakening. Not awakening — that is to forget the way home.

To indulge mouth and body, to gratify ear and eye, to vie and grapple with things — people call this joy. What joy? No sorrow is greater. To cast off the body, to extinguish mind and intellect, not to herd with things — people call this suffering. What suffering? No joy is greater. Therefore one who delights in suffering deepens in suffering; one who tastes joy as bitter finds joy daily melting away. So those who would walk the Way leave that and take this.

Heaven and earth toil not, yet accomplish transformation; the sage toils and so completes merit; the multitude labors and so carries affairs through. When affairs are carried through, one may rest; when merit is complete, one retires. Hence it is said: “When merit is complete and affairs accomplished, the body withdraws — this is the Way of Heaven.” The wealthy are arrogant; the highly placed are insolent; the much-accomplished boast; the great in ambition are mad; the superior in talent are proud. The deep in virtue are lowly; the solid in the Way are yielding.

Not understanding the borrowed conditions, one arbitrarily takes and rejects. The wind of consciousness fans and blows, vast and never still. The ocean’s waters are clear, yet wind raises waves. If the wind does not rise, how are waves born? If consciousness does not arise, how do the myriad conditions exist? Therefore for one who reaches the Way: not understanding, there is birth; understanding, there is no birth. Excellent!

If the source is not far, the stream is not long; if the Way is not great, the merit is not firm. Therefore the sage’s virtue covers the myriad beings and his merit flows through ten thousand ages, because his Way is great. One who possesses the great Way — who can breach it?

The eye contains heaven and earth, yet a mote of dust can rob it of its clarity; the mind encompasses the great void, yet a single thought can block its vastness. Know then that a single thought is the root of birth and death, the source of calamity. Therefore, knowing the minute and knowing the subtle, the sage keeps his guard.

One who trusts himself — though others do not trust him, he still trusts. One who does not trust himself — though others trust him, he still does not trust. Therefore self-trust is deep sincerity; the trust of others is easily deceived. Sincerity is called purity; deception is called sinking. Wisdom illumines, consciousness deludes; delusion gives rise to a thousand differences, while illumination abides alone. Therefore one who reaches the Way uses illumination to illumine delusion, and prizes wisdom, not consciousness.

Watch a man of the marketplace walking heedlessly: he stumbles into a hollow, yet he starts, flings out his arms and swears an oath — because he dislikes the mud on his shoes. But people today dwell in inferior virtue and are wholly at ease, never startled, never swearing. They make themselves lesser than the man of the marketplace and treat their own virtue as dung and stubble. Alas!

All know change as change and change accordingly, but they do not know that within change there abides the unchanging. If one knows the unchanging, then change cannot change him. If one does not know the unchanging, then even without change, when is he ever unchanged? Just look at the sage: his body follows the myriad beings, secretly passing through the four kinds of birth; in the welter of their doings he neither leads nor welcomes. That is to dwell in the unchanging while changing. What change is there? As for ordinary men, their form is like withered wood, yet their minds are like wind-blown dust; things have vanished from their sight, yet they still moan. That is no change — yet when are they ever unchanged?

Lying down, resting, sitting, sleeping — these ease the body. Cutting off entangling conditions — this eases the mind. When the body is at ease, the will declines; when the mind is at ease, the will becomes refined. Therefore one who nourishes the Way forgets the body and takes the mind as teacher; thus the Way becomes firm.

Heaven and earth are great because their capacity to contain makes them great; rivers and seas are deep because their readiness to receive makes them deep; the sage is honored because his taking in of filth and bearing of shame makes him honored. Therefore the sage, the more he tolerates, the greater; the lower he stoops, the more honored. Thus his Way penetrates a hundred kalpas and his blessings rise through all ages, and none contends with him.

To look on the people as my people — loving the good and hating the evil may yet be partial. To look on the people as my own mind — cherishing the good and pitying the evil is never untrue. Hence it is said: “Heaven and earth share one root; the myriad things are one body.” This is what is called universal benevolence.

He who sees forms is blind; he who sees seeing is clear-sighted. He who hears sounds is deaf; he who hears hearing is keen of ear. Thus when form is complete, seeing is complete; when sound is exhausted, hearing is exhausted — nothing fails to merge. Form and sound are both not; seeing and hearing do not abide. This is called the great penetration.

The myriad thoughts surge without cease; there is no way to meet the real. If one uses thoughts to still thoughts, the more one stills them the more they will not be stilled. If one uses a single thought to still the myriad thoughts, then without being stilled they are stilled of themselves. What I call the single thought is no-thought. One who can contemplate no-thought — though thoughts go on thinking, what thought is there in the end? Yet even so, to insist on real no-thought is a superfluity; men do not even know that it is a peg.

The substance of mind is originally empty; deluded thoughts do not exist. If one understands that delusions do not exist, then though they appear, they do not exist. If one does not understand that delusions do not exist, then though they do not exist, one still takes them as existing. Therefore deluded thoughts are like flowers in the sky; their root is a film upon the eye. Once the eye-fault is understood, the flowers are no longer taken as real; the substance of emptiness is forever quiescent.

When at rest one’s inner illumination seems present, but once one meets affairs it is gone — this is simply because mind and object are not yet merged and the dust of former experience is not yet finished, and so they obstruct. Therefore one who would reach the Way: if he has not understood the former dust, then even if thoughts and imaginings all stop, he is still tending toward stillness, and so he does not attain the supreme Way.

The essence is still, the function illumines; the function does not lose the essence. In illumining itself, it is still. The essence does not depart from the function; in stillness itself, it illumines. Thus the still essence is like the great void, and its illumining function like the white sun. Hence through ten thousand changes it suffers no loss, and no darkness is unillumined.

No beginning before, no end after; ten thousand kalpas are a single thought, the six directions a single emptiness. Beings and things share one track; great and small have one form. Day and night do not alter; death and life do not shift. This is called the constant. Yet one who embodies this, though a man, is heaven — who can make fault with him?

Affairs are small, principle is great. Affairs have a thousand differences; principle has but one flavor. One skilled in principle finds nothing outside the affair at hand; hidden and manifest, being and perishing are not two. Therefore the perfected person, the more he moves, the more still he is, and nowhere does he fail to dwell.

It cannot be attained by a mindless mind, nor sought by a mind that has mind. With mind one grasps existence; without mind one clings to nothingness. Both are wrong; then one stands aloof and independent. The great person has no counterpart because nothing can take hold of his mind.

When thought exists, things exist; when mind is empty, dharmas are empty. Thus if thought is like a hollow crucible, one is at ease in every condition; if the mind is like a round mirror, coming and going are always untroubled. One skilled in this, without leaving the ordinary, sits upright in the wondrous realm.

Great forgetting neither forgets nor leaves anything unforgotten. One who forgets with intent, the more he forgets, the more he fixes. The grasping man has not understood the Way; if he truly understood the Way, what would he not forget? Hence it is said: “Fish forget one another in water; men forget one another in the Way.”

The swimming fish does not know the sea; the flying bird does not know the sky; the common people do not know the Way. If they knew the Way, how could they be common? In my view, one who skillfully embodies the Way has a body like the fish and bird and a mind like sea and sky — he is near it.

In every movement and rest, every word and silence, the lifting of a brow, the blink of an eye, in drinking and in pecking, to left and to right — at no time is he unobservant. When observation is long, thought splits open; suddenly he is self-possessed. The self-possessed know it for themselves; no one else recognizes it.

The merit of heaven and earth does not discard a single blade of grass; the moisture of the vast sea does not reject a single drop; the substance of perfect clarity does not depart from a single thought. Know then how weighty is the matter of a single thought!

The true mind is vast beyond measure, this body minute beyond measure. Therefore one who has clarified the true mind looks back on this body as a wisp of cloud drifting in the great clear sky, coming and going at will, soaring free with nowhere to lodge. Because he has nowhere to lodge, he dwells in the world as a lodger.

To act with action — one cannot act. To act with non-action — one can act. Therefore the sage does nothing and yet nothing is left undone. What I call the sage’s non-action is simply acting without possessing the act — not like cold ashes and withered wood, utterly without action.

The great void wanders within my mind like a bubble in the sea — how much more heaven and earth within the great void, the myriad things within heaven and earth, this body within the myriad things, outer things within this body! Ah, how tiny! And because it is tiny, therefore it is great.

Heaven and earth are still; the myriad things are one. Guard stillness and know oneness, and the ten thousand affairs are finished. One who dwells in this Way is never at fault; because he is never at fault, all his doings and contrivings come to no loss. One who does not lose it is called a true person.

To be aloof and without counterpart is the great sameness. Where there is no sameness, self and things are two; self and things being two, opposition of form arises. Where there is opposition of form, nothing is more beset by dependence. How then is one aloof? In my view, one skilled in reaching the Way values the forgetting of both; when both are forgotten, self and things are one. Self and things being one, the opposition of form is forgotten. The opposition of form being forgotten, on what does one depend? Being without counterpart, therefore great; being great, therefore same. The greatly same is called a sage. Hence it is said: “Who but the sage can gather the myriad things into himself?”

Mountains, rivers and the great earth are one flavor of pure truth; the mind like perfect clarity, heaven and earth are void and still. Therefore one who has penetrated this: outwardly, whatever meets his eye can engage nothing; inwardly, turning back to look, there is not a single thing. Such is emptiness; emptiness leaves no trace. Things are but words. His body lodges within the world, his mind transcends beyond appearances.

When stillness is complete, the mind penetrates; when words are forgotten, the essence is understood. Therefore the person of penetration and understanding has a mind like a hanging mirror, a mouth as if his tongue were tied, a form like withered wood, a breath like frost and snow. Ah, who indeed is such a one? I would walk with him.

His form seems constrained, his inner depth vast and empty. His eyes seem not to see, his ears seem not to hear. Dim and dull, men look at him and think him foolish; like a man who has lost himself, he does not know who accompanies him. I beg to take him as my teacher.

All that the world contains is dim as a thing in a dream. In the dream it is not absent; after waking, what remains? Therefore without awakening, how can one transcend existence? Without transcending existence, how can one leave the world? What I call leaving the world is not leaving the world; leaving the world consists in leaving the world within the world. One who leaves the world within the world is called a perfected person.

Knowledge is the beginning; the utmost end is the finish. One spurs knowledge with wisdom, and wields the utmost with expedient means. Expedient means is that which engages existence. Engaging existence, one dwells in change. In antiquity there were those who, through ten thousand changes, never lost their rectitude, because the root was preserved. But those today who, lacking the root, boast themselves skilled in change — they are like men who bind themselves and then loose others; whoever sees them will surely spit, and even a child laughs aloud at them.

Direct arrival is called sudden; secret cultivation is called gradual. Direct arrival reaches the true; secret cultivation removes the false. If the true is not reached, the false is not removed; if the false is not removed, the true is not complete. From this, look at the false: is it not the obscuring of the true, the harm of the Way, the burden of virtue?

Perfect fusion and total embrace, vast and mutually interpenetrating; wholly affair, wholly principle; hidden and manifest beyond reckoning. One and many mutually contain; many and one mutually enter. Raise one and all is gathered, yet nothing hinders their array. Small and great are not different; ordinary and sage are not divided. Ever extinguished, ever illumining; ever arising, ever still. The mind cannot think it; speech cannot discuss it. In daily use and the ordinary there is never any lack; the constant is within it, and no journey is needed. This is called the utmost.

Great words carry the Way; small words carry names. Supreme words forget words. He who carries names stays near; he who carries the Way goes far; he who forgets words penetrates. Therefore the near is easily familiar, the far is easily slandered, and the penetrating is beyond reckoning. Because it is supreme, it is beyond reckoning. One who dwells in the beyond-reckoning is called divine transformation.

A single palm does not sound; without emptiness there is no echo; without counterpart there are no words. From this we see that words arise from dependence. Yet even so: to speak the word of no-words — the word is then no-word. No-words is what words cannot reach. In my view, one who would skillfully attain no-words must let words go. Once words are let go, no-words is attained. What words are there?

Fu Guangzhai of Liaocheng said: “Among what the world calls the books of the philosophers, are not Laozi and Zhuangzi the highest? Laozi’s words are terse and his meaning profound; Zhuangzi’s speech is strange and his thought far-reaching. Those who later discoursed on the Way took refuge in them. From Xunzi and Yangzi downward, none is fit to be compared. Is this Xu Yan — Prefatory Words — not of the company of Laozi and Zhuangzi? Its writing is brilliant and lucid, yet its purport is hard to name in words. Perhaps there are even points where Laozi and Zhuangzi fall short?” A doubter says: “You go too far. How could Laozi and Zhuangzi be equaled?” I say: “Truly Laozi and Zhuangzi cannot be equaled. Yet such sayings as ‘the valley spirit’ and ‘mixing with the dust,’ and ‘the beginning of doubt’ and ‘the dark pearl,’ seem to speak and yet not exhaust, and again seem to wish to speak yet find speech difficult. The Way is truly without limit. The Western Sage had no dharma to teach, yet he taught a dharma; in him speech is exhausted. Thus, looking at Laozi and Zhuangzi, one knows that the philosophers are not complete; looking at the Western Sage, one knows that Laozi and Zhuangzi are not complete. This Xu Yan’s purport comes from the Western Sage, while its writing resembles Laozi and Zhuangzi. Hence I said, ‘Perhaps there are points where Laozi and Zhuangzi fall short.’ Yet this too is words; where there are words, it is a preface. Hence it is named Prefatory Words. Take its words and seek what it does not say — that rests with the person. Otherwise, one might say that Hanshan is a man of today; what is remarkable about his Prefatory Words? He would fall short not only of Laozi and Zhuangzi but even of the philosophers.”
