The Master was at Mount Jing, receiving and meeting his disciples, speaking freely, talking on from sunrise — all of it the most intimate and direct guidance for benefiting beings after realization, and not to be scattered and lost. In my life I could grasp the purport but not memorize the words. The Master’s words were as deep and vast as waves, and I did not even raise this intention until ten days later, so I could no longer recall the whole. I began to set down headings in order and record the general outline; earlier talks, together with the subsequent separate instructions, are appended one by one to form the Dharma Talks at Mount Jing, so that they may be printed and given out widely and the Master’s compassionate spittle not be spent in vain. Master Danju and the great assembly are of one mind in this.
Recorded by the disciple Zhu Lu
This great matter must be discussed plainly and honestly if it is to be of use. Above all, do not crave the abstruse and wondrous; a flood of lips and tongue is called playing with the spirit.

If one does not enter this matter through investigation, one gains no strength. If one does not verify it against the teachings, one does not gain right view. If one is not forged in the crucible of conditions and circumstances, it is merely a matter of light and shadow at the gate. When the eight winds of adversity and favor come, one is shaken and carried off, unable to pass through. Enter through the Chan school, verify with the teachings, test by daily conditions — and simply be light and free amid conditions, with no mind that sticks: that is where mind-work gains strength. If one can examine oneself by conditions, one need not rely entirely on a good teacher’s words as the absolute method.

Bite firmly on the huatou — not in order to understand the huatou, but only to use the huatou to raise doubt and cut off deluded thought. The investigation must be carried on apart from the huatou itself. Only when doubt takes hold does it gain strength. The ancients said: “Three inches from the hook — why do you not speak?” Those before us set their minds on this. When doubt reaches the point where feeling and consciousness cannot arrive and words cannot reach, where it presses to the extreme, a little light and shadow bursts forth; this is called the samādhi of lightning. That is just the time to press forward, and one must not rejoice. If one takes this as it, one is satisfied with little, and one’s whole being is covered over by that speck of light and can never come forth again; whatever arises afterward, one is driven by it. Within the eighth consciousness are stored many lives’ habitual tendencies; when subtle seeds suddenly appear and no effort avails, one must borrow the power of mantra to dissolve them.

Question: Where do wisdom and consciousness differ? The very first thought, direct perception, is wisdom; as soon as it turns to the second, it is inference and falls into feeling and thought. Again: what comes tainted with feeling is consciousness; what comes untainted by feeling is wisdom. Biting firmly on the huatou is precisely seizing the road by which feeling and consciousness come, so that no second thought arises.

Investigation and awakening are not such difficult matters. Keep your breath unified for three months, and you will surely see where it settles. Above all, do not beforehand harbor a mind that awaits awakening; the moment you await awakening, you are waiting for awakening to come to you, and this very thing is a bar laid across your path, so that your practice can never enter. Again: this matter must be done by a fierce and courageous man.

One of sharp faculties has gained innate wisdom through many lives; meeting the right conditions in this life, he is finished on the spot. There are those who do not enter by investigation but need only preserve and carry it through, like the Sixth Patriarch. What of the dull-rooted? They need only consent to it themselves. The dull are not clever; they gain strength precisely from their dullness.

Bite firmly on the huatou; it is useful at every time. Even going up a mountain of knives or into a mass of fire, it is useful. There you gain the power of samādhi. If there is the slightest evasion, your whole body falls.

A Chan practitioner must not sit down on pure white ground; this is a pitfall for a thousand lives and ten thousand kalpas. Wishing to expose it for the assembly, I composed the Song of Carrying the Board.

The eye of the teachings and the eye of the school are originally not two eyes. Master Yongming, in presenting the school, took up the words of the teachings entirely to seal and confirm them, fearing that people would one-sidedly stray onto the road of no-meaning and misstep. Without the eye of the teachings, one falls into wrong views. In my commentaries on the Diamond, Lotus, Laṅkāvatāra, Śūraṅgama and other sutras, I picked out whatever burst forth where feeling and consciousness cannot reach and the road of meaning is cut off, wishing thereby to seal the school with the teachings; students should attain it for themselves.

During my time at the Eastern Sea, one evening as I sat, body and world became empty; the ocean seal emitted light and rivers and mountains quaked — I attained the corresponding wisdom. After a while I penetrated the crucial point of the Śūraṅgama, and it was suddenly before my eyes. I hurriedly lit a candle and wrote; my wrist could not pause, and by the end of the fifth watch the Śūraṅgama Hanging Mirror was complete. My attendant came out to check on me and, seeing the guttering candle on the desk, was astonished.
A bodhisattva makes benefiting beings his entire business. If he does not see through the various dharmas of the world, he cannot match the occasion and benefit beings.
In learning the Buddha’s way, first arouse the mind of great compassion, and take the breaking of self-attachment as the main thing.
Old koans, measured by people today with deluded thought, no longer meet point to point. Even if one understands and can speak of them, they lend no strength to one’s own practice.
To penetrate amid movement is easy to enter; entering amid stillness has no strength.
Entering through outer knowledge and views has no strength; entering through inner realization of one’s own nature gains strength.

Question: What of one who attains through conditions? Conditions are of two kinds: the condition of seeing and hearing is subject to regression; the condition of an actual state is not subject to regression, because the real and the insubstantial differ.
For ordinary beings, the patience of desire; for the two vehicles, the patience of birth; for bodhisattvas, the patience of non-arising; for the Buddha, the patience of quiescent extinction.

Only the one Buddha-view is right, yet there are bodhisattva-views, two-vehicle views, being-views and outsider views, all of them confused and mistaken. Therefore the World-Honored One used various expedients, solely to have them understand the one mind and enter right view, which is called the Buddha-view.
Understand that the mind of birth and death is quiescent, and you understand birth and death.
What is the upward path? There is only letting go.
The patriarchs’ words are living, every phrase. When students take them as fixed dharmas, every phrase is dead.
In daily practice, one need only see through deluded thoughts and not be used by them; there is no other place to apply the mind.
When you cannot empty anything, what then? Simply understand that it is false; then all can be emptied and all can be made light.
The bodhisattva dwells in the Land of Ultimate Bliss — what is he doing there? I want to drag him out.
The phrase “Namo Amitābha Buddha” is originally the same as a huatou; people today, however, turn it into going to the West.

That all is illusion everyone knows; one must have the capacity to master illusion before one is not turned by it. At Haiyin I once recalled the koan of the Sixth Patriarch and the man who came at midnight to cut off his head, and wished to learn his power of samādhi. Every night I opened the door and practiced visualization: if someone came to ask for my head, I would joyfully give it. So it was tonight, and so the next night. After a long time I felt a settled power of resolve. Then one night a thief was reported to have entered. I said, “Just call him in,” lit a candle and sat upright, with no fear in my heart. When the man reached the door, he crawled on the ground and dared not enter — a great tall fellow. I called out that there was nothing here, and ordered two hundred coins from the store to be given him. Had I not mastered it beforehand, I would have been thrown into panic.

Dwelling in the Wutai Mountains, the clamor was like a million men in fierce battle; there was not a single breath of peace. One day I listened where the spring rushed most violently, and after a moment I suddenly no longer heard it. The instant I raised the thought “Why?” I heard it again. So I sat for many days at the place of greatest tumult. After sitting long, the sound of the water became still. Thereafter the water’s sound never ceased, yet it was as if I did not hear it. After that I dwelt peacefully in the mountains and was never again stirred by clamor.

While I was at the Eastern Sea, the Empress Dowager sent a eunuch with a sum of silver, and I dared not refuse. I judged that I could not recklessly accept it for myself; reflecting that the region was suffering famine, I could use it to spread the Empress Dowager’s bounty. The eunuch objected. I told him I would inform the counties and have those who received the alms in that region make a register to report back; this was agreed. Later, when the two palaces heard of it, they were greatly pleased. And when I afterwards met with disaster, it was this very deed that helped me. Thus one knows that in the face of wealth one must not be careless.

When I was in Lingnan, I was not yet familiar with the ways of the people and kept a lofty distance, so that none could approach me freely; there was no one close to me. A small child wished to come near, yet always feared and ran from me. One day I learned the lion’s way of taming its cub: I forced myself to lie down and fondle him, giving him fruits and melons. Day by day he grew more familiar, and at last did not fear me. From then on people no longer shunned me, and came daily closer.

When I first went to pay my respects to a certain regional commander, I held my card in the courtyard, and for a long while he did not order me to rise and withdraw. I understood in my heart that I ought to announce my own name and present myself, yet I could not get it out of my mouth; it was as heavy as a thousand catties. When I could bear it no longer, I summoned my resolve and announced my name: “So-and-so presents himself.” Only then could I rise and leave. The next day when I came again it was the same, and for a whole year he granted me no indulgence. Others said he was a military man — how could he know to break convention in receiving a good teacher? At last, on the day we were to go together to visit the governor’s office, the commander prepared a boat with vegetarian food and fruit laid out like a guest’s seat, invited me aboard, bowed, and saluting me to the seat of honor, said: “It is not that I could not indulge you; I knew you had proud bones, and wished thereby to complete you.” We talked joyfully knee to knee before parting. Then I sighed to think how many deep-hearted men there are among officials — why ask whether they are military?

If one reads without careful personal verification, one does not get the use of it. When I was annotating Laozi, I came to “The Way of Heaven — is it not like the drawing of a bow?” I spent several more days but could not find where it fit. So I borrowed a bow and string from someone, drew it and hung it on the wall, and watched it sitting and lying. Two days later I suddenly understood that “drawing” is spoken in contrast to “slackening.” When the bow is slack, the grip stands high with slack to spare and the tips hang low and insufficient, so it is useless. When it is drawn and used, then the high is pressed down and the low raised, the grip is reduced and the tips supplied, upper and lower evenly balanced, and one can hit the mark. The Way of Heaven takes movement entirely as its function; it gives and does not receive — this fits exactly. As for the two lines “The heavy is the root of the light,” I also examined them for several years, not daring to explain them carelessly. It happened to be on the day I was traveling south, sitting alone in a boat with nothing to occupy my feelings, that the meaning of heavy and light, stillness and restlessness, appeared suddenly before my eyes. Only then did I understand the purport of the Supreme One’s words: it is seen only after one has tested it in one’s own body. One cannot say that the stale words on paper have no true flavor. Thus my one commentary on the Daodejing took thirteen years before it left the manuscript — it was no careless work.

When I compose a commentary, it must be that I gather my spirit and enter contemplation, and my understanding accords with the Buddha’s mind; only when a hint suddenly bursts forth of itself do I commit it to paper. If it involves discursive thought, it is of no use.

It is said: “If the sage does not appear in the world, ten thousand ages are as a long night.” Therefore our original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, manifested in a royal palace, left home at the Snowy Mountains, practiced austerities for six years, awakened to the Way and became Buddha, and taught at the Deer Park to save beings. Before the Buddha appeared in the world, there were ninety-six kinds of outsiders in India, each establishing its own house and gate and all claiming to be teachers. When the Buddha accomplished the Way and taught, those outsiders one by one took refuge, left home, became the Buddha’s disciples, practiced according to the teaching and realized the fruit of arhatship. Thus the assembly on Vulture Peak, twelve hundred and fifty in number, were all of the company of outsiders. At that time, those who had faith in the Buddha took refuge in Buddha, Dharma and Saṅgha and practiced as taught; those without faith were startled and doubtful, and even suffered all kinds of demonic harm and slander, falling into evil paths beyond counting. Know then that in lands today where the Buddhadharma has not spread, it is as in the time before the Buddha appeared: wise and foolish, worthy and unworthy, though their doubt and faith differ, all fail to know the original intent of our Buddha’s appearance and the graduated expedient rules for saving beings. Therefore I now briefly set out the stages of the expedient means for converting beings, so that those who have not heard and do not believe the Buddhadharma may know that we who are monks — the Dharma gate of converting beings — cannot be entered by any single deed, single practice or single gate. Hence it is said: “Expedient means have many gates; the return to the source has no second.” In sum, the forty-nine years were all in accordance with the order of faculties, great and small, shallow and deep — what is called “teaching does not skip grades.” I hope you will understand this fully and not call it common talk.
A Buddha appears in the world for the sake of one great matter: to open and demonstrate to beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and cause them to awaken and enter it. This one matter alone; there is no other. What is called the one great matter means that beings should know that birth and death are the one great matter. The Buddha’s knowledge and vision is the Buddha-nature that each and every being originally possesses. Because they are deluded about this Buddha-nature, birth and death arise. Now, to escape the suffering of birth and death, one must take the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as the first principle. Is this not the Buddha’s appearing in the world precisely to point directly at the human mind and enable the seeing of the nature and the becoming of Buddha? In that case the path of Chan, of awakening the mind, did not wait for Bodhidharma’s coming from the West — the Buddha appeared especially for this matter. Yet, alas, beings through kalpas past, with greed, hatred, delusion and craving, afflictions and evil views, have been deeply deluded and cannot bear the sudden revelation of the great dharma of awakening the mind. Therefore the One Vehicle dharma was divided and taught as three. Hence the gradual establishment of the three vehicles, called the small, middle and great vehicles. For those who could not bear even the small vehicle’s dharma, the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds were established as good fruits of gods and humans, so that they might at least avoid falling into the sufferings of the three evil paths — hell, hungry ghosts and animals. Hence it is said: “If the five precepts are not kept, the road to gods and humans is cut off.” Now, as disciples of the Buddha, we revere and follow the Buddha’s teaching and take the saving of beings as our work. If we do not use graduated expedients to lead and draw them into the Way, but all at once display the great dharma, we cause them instead to give rise to doubt and slander and to bring on themselves the suffering of the three evil paths — thus turning sweet cream into poison. That is the fault of not guiding well. Therefore, following what the Buddha established: the lay good man is called upāsaka, the lay good woman is called upāsikā, and they should keep the five precepts to cultivate the good fruits of gods and humans. The five precepts for the laity are:
1. Not to kill. (This precept brings the reward of long life in the future, of agreeable and harmonious kin, and of flourishing descendants in the present.)

2. Not to steal. (Whatever is taken without being given is called theft. This precept brings the reward of great wealth in future lives, ample clothing and food, and the fulfillment of all one seeks.)

3. Not to commit sexual misconduct. (To arouse lust toward one who is not one’s own wife or consort is called misconduct. This precept brings the reward of a faithful and virtuous spouse in future lives, a loving father and filial sons, and harmony among the six kinds of kin.)

4. Not to speak falsely. (Whatever is untrue, or sets two parties at odds, is called false speech. This precept brings the reward of wisdom surpassing others in future lives, words that are true, and hearers who believe and practice as taught.)

5. Not to drink alcohol. (Alcohol clouds and confuses the nature, driving men mad and breeding disaster; it is the root of all evil. This precept brings the reward of bright and penetrating wisdom and transcendent insight in the future.)

The five precepts above were specially established by our Buddha when he first appeared in the world, for lay people living in the world, so that people might cultivate the cause according to the precepts, not waste this life, avoid falling into evil paths, and in future lives not lose the human body but obtain long life, great wealth and descendants, a prosperous household, and the reward of cultured distinction. All those today who hold high office and noble rank, who are rich and abundant, who are intelligent and successful, have come from practicing the five precepts. These five precepts are the five constants of the Confucian school: not killing is benevolence; not stealing is righteousness; no sexual misconduct is propriety; not drinking alcohol is wisdom; not speaking falsely is trustworthiness. Thus the Buddhadharma is of aid to the kingly way: converting people by the five precepts means no litigation, fewer punishments, well-ordered households and simple customs. This is the very first rite of converting beings established by our Buddha. People of the world today who do not know the Buddhadharma, who have no mind to love goodness at all but instead give rise to views slandering Buddha, Dharma and Saṅgha, willingly choose delusion and bring suffering on themselves. There is also another kind: though they eat vegetarian food, they do not know the true path of Buddhadharma practice, and follow the heterodox teachers of the Non-Action sect, who do not revere the Buddha, the patriarchs, heaven and earth, are unfilial to their parents, do not burn incense or bow to the Three Jewels, and devote themselves wholly to heterodox practices and doctrines, blindly leading the blind, gathering to talk wildly and calling it transmitting the Dharma, entirely unaware that there is a true path of practice, and instead slandering Buddha, Dharma and Saṅgha, stubbornly holding on and refusing to change. These are the most foolish of people, and pitiable; they are precisely those whom the imperial decree now orders to be prohibited. I only hope that the wise and noble gentlemen of this age will distinguish clearly between heterodox and orthodox, right and wrong, and whenever they meet such people, immediately instruct them, leading them to abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox. This not only protects the Buddhadharma but also aids the king’s civilizing work. Yet whether one studies the heterodox or the orthodox, it is always a single thought of good intention; it is a pity that they do not know it is heterodox and so fall by mistake. If they now recognize their error, why not abandon those heterodox followers and become truly good people, good citizens of a sage age?

The five precepts above are the Buddhadharma’s cause and effect for cultivating the human path. It further establishes the ten wholesome paths of conduct as the cause and effect of gods and humans. The ten wholesome deeds are:
1. The body has three evil actions: killing, stealing and sexual misconduct. If these three evils are cut off, they are called the three wholesome paths.
2. The mouth has four evil actions: false speech, idle talk, divisive speech and harsh speech. If these four are cut off, they are called the four wholesome paths.
3. The mind has three evil actions: greed, hatred and delusion. If these three are cut off, they are called the three wholesome paths.

The ten evils above are what ordinary people use daily without knowing it. If one can now cut off these ten evils, they are called the ten wholesome deeds, the cause of rebirth in heaven, and one becomes a person of pure goodness. These ten wholesome practices are the Confucian way of rectifying the mind, making the will sincere and cultivating the self. If one can truly practice them, one becomes a sage or a worthy in this life and will surely be reborn in a heavenly palace in the next, receiving supreme and wondrous bliss. This is an utterly true practice — why are people of the world so deluded as not to know it, and instead turn wholly to heterodox paths as if they were gain? Do they not betray their own minds?

The five precepts and ten wholesome deeds above were established by our Buddha especially for lay people living in the world, requiring them to cultivate the cause accordingly and not lose the blessings of gods and humans. This is proclaimed by the golden mouth, words that are no lie. If one does not cultivate accordingly, it is altogether a heterodox path, not right practice. Even if one is willing to practice bitterly, there is no benefit; one only adds to the fruit of suffering. This is called casting away suffering by means of suffering; our Buddha has grieved deeply over it. The teachings of the Five Books and Six Volumes now in the world are the work of heterodox and wicked men who falsely claim to be teachers, stealing the words of the Buddha and patriarchs and mixing in vulgar worldly sayings to delude the ignorant. What is called the heterodox path confounding the true — these are exactly the people whom the present imperial edict prohibits. Lay people who already have a mind to love goodness: why do they not take refuge in the Three Jewels, but must fall into these heterodox teachings? How is that a wise person?

Again, observe the good-hearted men of today: having already taken refuge in the Three Jewels, they rely on their own worldly cleverness and sharp wit, and so give rise to a low and inferior demonic mind. They slight the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds and do not practice them; they take a liking for Chan as the supreme vehicle, yet do not cultivate the three karmas. Taking the ready-made koans of the patriarchs, they read a few, keep them in their breast, and then display a glib tongue, brandishing the Chan thrust at every turn, taking this as their own wonderful awakening, holding it to be right and wholly unaware that it is wrong. Moreover they slander the Mahāyāna scriptures as words not worth taking up, and mock monks who truly practice as followers of the small vehicle, wantonly giving rise to all kinds of wrong views and wholly disbelieving in cause and effect, offense and blessing. They even slight the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha, never realizing that they have fallen into the pit of delusion and karmic obstruction while wife and children gather about them and all sufferings and burning afflictions sear them; and they recklessly point to what is before their eyes as the Way. Such foolish people are greatly to be pitied. Since they have a single thought turned upward, why do they not truly and solidly do some practical work? As it is said: “Better to have practiced one part than to have spoken ten.” Such wild talk is like a poor man falsely claiming to be emperor and bringing execution on himself. Is it not grievous? I exhort the good gentlemen of the world, sharp-witted and keen-rooted, who aspire to escape birth and death: weigh your own faculties. Chan investigation is indeed the upward step, but the Buddha and patriarchs spoke it especially for those of the very highest faculties. Let each of you examine himself: are you truly of the very highest faculties? Can you truly awaken at every point? Can you truly finish a hundred kalpas of birth and death on the spot? If your faculties are not the very highest, then you should measure your own strength and devote yourself single-mindedly to the Pure Land gate, dedicating the merit toward the West and vowing to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, forever forsaking the suffering of the Sahā world. In this one Dharma gate, from ancient times monks and laypeople without number have cultivated the cause and escaped birth and death by relying on it. It is what is called “ten thousand practice, ten thousand go” — the most steady and safe, the great Dharma gate in which not a hair’s breadth goes wrong. The patriarch said: “There is only the shortcut of practice: simply recite Amitābha Buddha.” By this Dharma gate no one is misled at all. If you can put down body and mind and practice accordingly, the rules you should follow are briefly set out below.

1. The Pure Land gate is often spoken of by scholars and officials as designed specifically for those of middle and lower faculties. They do not realize that this gate embraces all three faculties universally, rejecting no capacity, and is the most vast; moreover it is simple and easy to practice. Even among the patriarchs of old, not a few turned their minds toward the Pure Land after awakening to the Way — great patriarchs such as Yongming and Zhongfeng, and not one alone. But in practicing Buddha-recitation there are differences of upper, middle and lower faculties, and so the nine grades of the Pure Land differ according to faculties.

Now there are three kinds of Pure Land: first, the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light; second, the Land of Real Reward and Adornment; third, the Land of Expedient Transformation with Remainder — this being the Land Where Sages and Ordinary Beings Dwell Together. These three lands differ in the causes cultivated, and so the fruits they yield differ. Let me speak of them briefly.

1. The Land of Eternally Quiescent Light is what the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment calls the Treasury of Great Light. In it sages and ordinary beings are equal, and dependent and principal retributions are undivided; there is only the Buddha’s dharmakāya, clear and eternally quiescent — the realm of the dharmakāya realized by all Buddhas. This is dwelt in only by those patriarchs from of old who in a single thought suddenly awakened to the dharmakāya, wondrously merged with the same substance and entered the Buddha’s realm. This is precisely the Pure Land of those of the very highest faculties; how can it be lightly regarded as intended for those of middle and lower capacity?

2. The Land of Real Reward and Adornment is the twenty-fold Lotus Treasury World — the wondrous land of endless adornment, commensurate with the measure of the dharma-realm, which our Vairocana Buddha produced by practicing through vast kalpas. It is what the Avataṃsaka Sūtra describes as world-adornments layer upon layer without end. This is the Pure Land dwelt in by the reward-body Buddha, where he turns the great Dharma wheel solely for bodhisattvas of the ten grounds; the two vehicles, the hearers, neither see nor hear it. It is also the Pure Land of which those in the Lotus assembly who received predictions will, after cultivating the cause for many kalpas, come to experience one portion. This is by no means easily or commonly reached.

3. The Land of Expedient Transformation with Remainder, also called the Land Where Sages and Ordinary Beings Dwell Together, is precisely the division into nine grades; it is the transformation land of Amitābha Buddha. The Lotus Treasury World has twenty tiers: from the first tier, worlds in number like motes of dust in a Buddha-land surround it, small below and large above, like an inverted stūpa, and from there upward each tier doubles and increases, up to the thirteenth tier. Now this Sahā world is the central presiding land of the thirteenth tier; the Land of Ultimate Bliss stands exactly equal to Sahā, from its center to the west to the edge of its petals. Hence it is said to be beyond ten trillion Buddha-lands and to stand level with Sahā. For among the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, only Sahā is foul and evil: earth, stones and mountains filled with mixed filth; the three evil paths and the eight difficulties where all sufferings gather; it is called the World of Endurance. Its beings are hard and stiff, the most difficult to tame and transform. Therefore our Śākyamuni Buddha, though he converted and guided gods and humans by the ten wholesome deeds, left them still within birth and death, not yet out of the round of rebirth. And if they investigated Chan to awaken the mind, sudden awakening was again difficult. So he established the one gate of reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking birth in the Pure Land, called “crossing the three realms horizontally.” By relying on the power of Amitābha Buddha’s vows made while cultivating the cause — “If there are beings in the worlds of the ten directions who can recite my name and are not born in my land, I vow not to become a Buddha” — by relying on this vow-power, whoever recites the Buddha’s name will certainly be welcomed by Amitābha and born in that Pure Land. Hence it is easy to be born there. Now this Pure Land is opened into nine grades. If one has investigated Chan and awakened the mind but cannot yet forget mind and objects, one is born in the top-upper grade. If one recites the Buddha’s name single-mindedly without distraction, one is born in the top-middle grade. If one investigates Chan without awakening, but holds the name purely and diligently, adorned with the ten thousand practices, one is born in the top-lower grade. If one cultivates the ten thousand practices, upholds the Mahāyāna scriptures, single-mindedly holds the name and vows to be born there, one is born in the three middle grades. If one keeps the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds purely, single-mindedly recites the Buddha’s name, makes vows and dedicates the merit — whether monk or lay — one is generally born in the three lower grades. Though such a one has not cut off afflictions, simply by being born in that land, seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, he dwells on the ground of non-regression and never again falls into the birth and death of the three realms. From there he makes vows and returns to the three realms to save beings, coming and going at ease, no longer detained by the afflictions of birth and death. Hence Chan Master Yongming said: “If only one sees Amitābha, why worry about not awakening?” This one Dharma gate can be accomplished with a lifetime of sincere devotion; once born there, one at once escapes birth and death and forever leaves the round of rebirth. Such a direct and swift Dharma gate — why fear it and not practice it, why slight it? Truly, to end birth and death by Chan investigation is hard; to end birth and death by Buddha-recitation is easy. It only requires that the person’s single thought be true and earnest, willing to bear hardship. From ancient times those born in the Pure Land are beyond measure or number, yet people see it with their own eyes and do not believe. What other dharma could they believe? I now exhort the wise and lofty, sharp scholars: believe in your own mind, and do not falsely believe heterodox doctrines. Even within the Dharma gate there are many who practice both Chan and Pure Land: as Yongming said, reciting the Buddha’s name and investigating Chan, investigating Chan and reciting the Buddha’s name — what is called “having both Chan and Pure Land is like a tiger with horns; in this life a teacher of men, in the future a Buddha-patriarch.” This too is the highest practice, as far from those who falsely claim to have awakened and fall into the great lie as heaven is from an abyss.

Now all beings, having deluded themselves about the Buddha-nature they originally possess, fall into the birth and death of the three realms and revolve amid the suffering of the six destinies. That they sink for long kalpas and cannot escape is entirely because greed, hatred, delusion and craving feed the evil karma of lust, killing, stealing and falsehood. Casting off one body and receiving another, they take sexual desire as the very substance of their lives; life after life, parents, wives, children and the six kinds of kin entangle them in affection, and they are burned by the great fire of the three realms, and not one among them can escape. Therefore our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha, from the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light, aroused the mind of great compassion to save beings from suffering. Forsaking the bliss of the Dharma of his own nature, he descended from the Tuṣita Heaven, came down into the royal palace, entered his mother’s womb, and then forsook parents, wife and child; he cut off the world’s deep and heavy bonds of affection and at once cast aside the rank of the golden-wheel king. He went into the Snowy Mountains, shaved off hair and beard, and for six years endured cold and hunger in ascetic practice, until he awakened to the Way and became Buddha. This is the first model of leaving home for the sake of birth and death. After becoming Buddha he again met with demonic harm, suffering the calamities of the golden spear and the horse-fodder slander, enduring all things, risking body and life, suffering without limit the assaults of demons and enemies; and he taught the Dharma for forty-nine years with only a single thought of compassion, to save beings and rescue them from suffering. This one matter alone; there was no other. Thus the disciples in the assembly on Vulture Peak, twelve hundred and fifty in number, were all the heroes and champions of that age; learning what the Buddha practiced, each forsook the world’s parents, wife, children and affections, practiced according to the Buddha’s teaching, awakened to and understood affection, escaped birth and death, and realized the fruit of arhatship. Even Ānanda, the Buddha’s cousin, followed him in leaving home and shared the assembly’s hardships. This is the model of the disciples whom our Buddha saved by their leaving home. When the Buddha was in the world, the disciples who came to him to leave home did not know the method of practice, so the Buddha established precepts according to circumstances, to make them stop evil and guard against wrongdoing and gain right cultivation. Thus for those newly gone forth, called śrāmaṇera, ten precepts were established; for fully ordained monks, two hundred and fifty precepts; for women who leave home, called bhikṣuṇī, five hundred great precepts. And for kings, ministers, officials and laymen, for the four assemblies of lay and monastic, to advance in the great bodhisattva precepts, there is the Brahmā Net Sūtra, which sets forth ten major and forty-eight minor precepts. These precepts and rules are the family law of our Buddha’s Dharma gate. Hence it is said: “If a person receives the Buddha’s precepts, he at once enters the rank of all Buddhas.” If one is a monk and does not receive the precepts, one is called a bald thief, stealing the Buddha’s robe, trafficking in the Tathāgata, not a disciple of the Buddha. This is how exacting it is for a monk to uphold the Dharma. Now when the Buddha was in the world, human life lasted a hundred years, and the Buddha’s span should have been a hundred years; but thinking of the disciples of the Dharma-ending age who have no blessing, he remained in the world only eighty years, leaving twenty years of unexhausted blessing to the sons and grandsons of later generations. Therefore the disciples of today, in the four kinds of offerings they receive, all enjoy a portion of the merit from our Buddha’s white-hair light. Even a grain of rice or a stalk of vegetables from a donor, the smallest share of giving, is a field of blessing left by the Buddha. Yet those who now enter the Dharma gate as monks do not even know who the Buddha is, nor what they themselves are about; they do not know why they forsook parents, abandoned wife and children, shaved off hair and beard, and instead of staying in a lay home dwell in a temple; nor do they know, since they neither plow nor weave, where their clothing and food come from. They only say they have their own ability and have converted donors to make offerings. Still less do they know that a donor’s faith, bought with fat and blood, is hard to digest, and that in the future they will drag the plow and pull the harrow, bear the bit and carry the saddle, and suffer the pain of repayment. This is what everyone alike is blind to and does not know. If one uses offerings in this way, yet can at least roughly keep the precepts, recite sutras and the Buddha’s name and keep to one’s own place, that is still tolerable. How much worse, then, those who wholly ignore the monastic body, do not receive the precepts, indulge body and mind, cling to lay relatives, come and go without restraint, do not avoid reproach, and even break the law and violate prohibitions, wholly unaware that they are wrong — and these are not of one kind only. They do not even know why they left home, why they forsook the world, why they shaved off hair and beard. Not only do they not know the matter of practice; the very mind of burning incense, bowing to the Buddha and revering the Three Jewels is utterly forgotten. They muddle through a lifetime, living as if drunk and dreaming, wholly unaware that there is a true path of practice for those who have left home. And if anyone does see it, they turn it into something wrong. These are the most pitiable of all. The Buddha said: “The three evil paths and hells are not suffering; to lose the human body beneath the monk’s robe — that is suffering.” In short, they do not know what a monk is. Hence the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters says:

The Buddha said: “You bhikṣus, every morning you should stroke your own head. If you are willing to stroke your own head, you will turn back and examine yourselves: why is it that you have no hair and beard?” Because they do not know the rules of leaving home in the Buddhadharma, teachers do not become teachers and disciples do not become disciples; high and low are utterly divided, and they herd together like birds and beasts. They know only that clothing and food are urgent, and are wholly unaware that there is the matter of birth and death; they do not fear the suffering of the three evil paths in the future. In the world this custom has become the fashion and is taken as normal. Even those who leave their villages to wander as pilgrims, knowing only that there is gruel and rice in the monasteries, are utterly ignorant of the Buddhadharma and the Chan Way. These too are greatly to be pitied. Alas! The age is far from the sage, and the Dharma gate has fallen into decay to such a degree that it cannot be saved. Yet even so, in a village of ten households there must be loyalty and trustworthiness; and today, everywhere among the mountains, how could there be no heroes and champions of spirit? In each region, if only one or two are willing to arouse their minds and rise up, there will naturally be an opportunity for transformation. Therefore I now hope that those among the monasteries who have aspiration will each reflect and turn back, bear in mind the great matter of birth and death, bitterly amend former faults, and arouse a single thought directed toward the Way. At the beginning of arousing the mind, one should first seek out and request a good teacher and receive the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera. If one keeps the ten precepts without violation, one advances to the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu, examining each and every precept item in detail; and further, one advances to receive the great bodhisattva precepts of the Brahmā Net. For the teaching established by the Buddha takes the three studies of precepts, samādhi and wisdom as the root of becoming Buddha: it is said that from precepts samādhi arises, and from samādhi wisdom arises; these are the three undefiled studies. The marks of the various precepts are fully recorded in the precept scriptures; please examine them yourselves — they need not be listed in detail. After one has received the precepts, whether dwelling alone or following the assembly, one must recite the precept text before the Buddha every half month. If one has violated them, one confesses before the assembly, mends one’s faults and makes a new start; then body and mind are purified and karmic obstructions dissolved — this is the essential way out of suffering. Once one can keep the precepts as the root of practice, one should draw near to the Buddhadharma. Even if one cannot go out to hear lectures elsewhere, one should arouse one’s own mind and single-mindedly recite the Mahāyāna scriptures — the Avataṃsaka, Lotus, Perfect Enlightenment, Śūraṅgama and other great sutras — to plant the causes and conditions of prajñā. Or if one aspires to devote oneself to the one gate of the Western Pure Land, then Buddha-recitation is the primary practice and reciting the Mahāyāna scriptures the auxiliary; one makes vows and dedicates the merit at the six periods, seeking to escape the bitter destinies of birth and death. Thus alone is one not unworthy of the immense cause of leaving home, and does not waste this life. If there is one of the very highest faculties who arouses the mind to leave worldly karma behind, wanders with a staff to consult teachers, and resolves to investigate the great matter of birth and death beneath his own feet, he need only single-mindedly raise one thought and seek nothing outside. This again is the faculty of the supreme One Vehicle. Yet if only one arouses a willing mind, there will surely be a time of clarity and awakening; it depends on each person’s faculties and aspiration. As said above, keeping precepts, practicing, reciting sutras and reciting the Buddha’s name — even if one cannot suddenly awaken to one’s own mind, one does not waste the time, nor fail the cause of leaving home. But to drift idly and indulge one’s feelings, and to accomplish nothing until death — is that not greatly grievous? To waste this life and fall into the three evil paths, then one does not know when one will again raise one’s head.

The methods of practice for lay and monastic set out above, though they differ in depth, are the dharma taught in the first twenty years after our Buddha appeared in the world. The Buddha taught for forty-nine years, and the dharma he taught had three vehicles: the small, the middle and the great. In the first twenty years he taught only the doctrine of existence, called the small vehicle: that there is the suffering of birth and death in the three realms to escape, a two-vehicle nirvāṇa to seek, the cause and effect of the good paths of gods and humans, and the cause and effect of evil karma in the three evil paths; that all dharmas are truly existent. Hence the dharma of the Four Noble Truths. “Truth” means the real. The four truths are suffering, origination, cessation and the path. It means that there is truly and really suffering to be endured; origination is greed, hatred, delusion and craving, the afflictions — these afflictions are the cause of all suffering and can summon its fruit, so it is said that there is truly and really an origination of affliction to be cut off; cessation is the one-sided emptiness of the two vehicles’ nirvāṇa beyond the three realms, and by escaping birth and death one realizes the bliss of this nirvāṇa, so it is said that there is truly and really a nirvāṇa to be realized; the path is the method of practice cultivated by the two-vehicle people — hating suffering, cutting off origination, longing for cessation, cultivating the path. These are the eight renunciations and the five contemplations for stilling the mind: contemplating the body as impure, feeling as suffering, mind as impermanent, dharmas as without self; and there are also the contemplations of universal and particular mindfulness. This is called the dharma of escaping suffering cultivated by small faculties, and is named the teaching of the small vehicle.
Again, for those of somewhat sharper faculties there is the middle vehicle: expanding the former four truths, the Buddha taught the dharma of the twelve causes and conditions — ignorance conditions formations, formations condition consciousness, consciousness conditions name and form, name and form condition the six sense bases, the six bases condition contact, contact conditions feeling, feeling conditions craving, craving conditions grasping, grasping conditions becoming, becoming conditions birth, birth conditions old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering and distress. These are called the twelve links of existence. These twelve links cover the cause and effect of the three periods: the two links of the past are cause — ignorance and formations; the five links of the present are fruit — from consciousness to feeling; the three links of the present are cause — craving, grasping and becoming; the two links of the future are fruit — birth, old age, death, grief and suffering. “Condition” means to draw forth: the cause and effect of the three periods revolving, each drawing forth the next. For a person of middle faculties, contemplating these twelve causes and conditions, there are two gates, that of the flow and that of return and extinction: from ignorance to old age and death is the gate of the flow; if ignorance ceases, then the twelve links all cease together — the gate of return and extinction. Contemplating them in reverse and in forward order, one awakens to non-arising and realizes the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, one enlightened for himself. This is the dharma of the middle vehicle. These two vehicles’ dharmas were taught for twenty years; because faculties were dull and inferior and could not bear the great, they were expedient. After these twenty years, when faculties had gradually become more open, the Buddha then taught the dharma of the six perfections practiced by great-vehicle bodhisattvas: giving, keeping precepts, patience, vigor, meditation and wisdom. These six are practiced by Mahāyāna bodhisattvas and are named the great vehicle. In cultivating these six perfections, one solely saves beings below and seeks the Buddha-fruit above. Among these six, prajñā is the master; therefore in his second period the Buddha taught the Prajñā sutras for twenty-two years. These sutras are the most numerous: those that came to this land are the eight divisions of Prajñā, six hundred fascicles in all. These sutras speak purely of the wisdom of prajñā’s true emptiness, refuting the earlier two-vehicle view of the existence of birth and death and nirvāṇa; they extensively set forth the six perfections and even the four truths and twelve causes, all taking prajñā’s true emptiness as the ultimate standard and washing away the earlier attachment to existence. Thus the Diamond and Heart Sutras are the summit of the Prajñā teaching. The emptiness grasped by the earlier two vehicles was one-sided emptiness, the so-called emptiness of annihilation; this prajñā, by contrast, is the true emptiness of actuality. The Buddha’s three contemplations of emptiness, the provisional and the middle are the wondrous gate to becoming Buddha; yet this one Prajñā sutra speaks only of the one contemplation of emptiness, and so it is the initial gate for entering the great vehicle and the wondrous dharma for the bodhisattvas’ practice. The Sanskrit “prajñā” means wisdom. Therefore bodhisattvas benefit beings with wisdom as the head. It is said: without wisdom, expedient means become a bond; with wisdom, expedient means liberate. Now although this one gate of the contemplation of emptiness is contained in the eight divisions of Prajñā, its essential point is contained wholly in the fourteen lines of the Heart Sutra; and the whole Heart Sutra is contained in the single sentence “he illumined the five aggregates as empty,” which exhausts its meaning; and in that single sentence, if one sets to work, it is contained in the single word “illumined.” This is the simplest and most essential dharma gate. Yet in Chan practice the very first work of the mind is only the one word “illumined.” This one-word dharma gate our Buddha waited a full thirty years before teaching. From this we see that the dharma of cultivating the mind is hardly something ordinary beings can easily speak of or easily practice. This one-word dharma gate is called teaching the bodhisattvas; it is the dharma of the great vehicle. The original intent of the Buddha’s appearing in the world was simply to cause all beings to become Buddha, with no other matter. Even the teaching of a whole lifetime spoken over forty-nine years, now the great canon, is altogether the dharma gate for learning to become Buddha, the expedient means for becoming Buddha. Though there are the six perfections and ten thousand practices and many various gates, the essential meaning is only that the three contemplations are the root of becoming Buddha. The three contemplations are emptiness, the provisional and the middle way. In the whole teaching of a lifetime only the three contemplations are spoken. If we trace from the beginning to prajñā, only then was the one gate of the contemplation of emptiness taught. From this we know the dharma is not easy to teach, nor easy to enter.
Yet at the Prajñā assembly the two-vehicle people who heard the dharma there all held that prajñā was not within their wisdom and could not digest it at all. Though they had personally received the Buddha’s teaching for thirty years, they still did not believe or enter. How much less the evil-karma ordinary beings of today, who speak of emptiness with every mouth, wildly expounding the dharma of emptiness, saying there is no Buddha and no patriarch, no practice and no realization, and then call themselves people of the very highest faculties — are they not greatly arrogant and absurd? Only after the Buddha had taught prajñā’s contemplation of true emptiness did he then teach the contemplation of the provisional. The sutra of this contemplation is the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, which teaches the gate of consciousness-only. It says that when the Tathāgatagarbha is deluded it is called ālaya-consciousness; relying on this ālaya, which has three aspects, the body, the world and all the mountains, rivers, earth, beings and worlds arise as provisional dharmas, being shadows transformed by consciousness-only, like images in a mirror or the moon in water — existing yet unreal; hence they are called provisional. Question: Why did the Buddha teach the contemplation of the provisional? Answer: Because the earlier two-vehicle people grasped nirvāṇa as truly existent and so fell into one-sided emptiness, the Buddha taught prajñā’s true emptiness to refute the view that grasps existence and to cause them to contemplate prajñā’s true emptiness of actuality. Again, there was a class of bodhisattvas who delighted in emptiness excessively and grasped mere emptiness without being able to engage existence, refusing to save beings; so the Buddha taught that the body, mind and world of all beings are entirely transformations of consciousness-only, wholly provisional dharmas, and by this gate of consciousness-only reconciled emptiness and existence, intending to reveal the existence that is emptiness and the emptiness that is existence, and to point directly at consciousness-only to realize suchness. This is the gate teaching the earlier bodhisattvas to leave emptiness and enter the provisional to save beings. Hence this one contemplation is set forth in such sutras as the Saṃdhinirmocana and the Ghanavyūha. When these sutras were taught, the great-faculty bodhisattvas could already believe and receive them; but the small-faculty two vehicles after all did not dare to enter the world to benefit beings. So the Buddha taught the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, in which the layman Vimalakīrti manifests as a householder with wife and children, and on the pretext of inquiring after his illness converses with Mañjuśrī on the dharma gate of non-duality, rebuking the two vehicles and stirring up in them the mind to enter the world and save beings. This teaching is called “rebuking the partial and censuring the small, praising the great and extolling the perfect,” a minor inconceivable dharma gate, to dispel the narrow and inferior views of the two vehicles. This was our Buddha’s deep compassion and great pity, using all kinds of expedients and skillful means for small-faculty people to lead them into the great vehicle. Thus we know that the bodhisattva’s affair of entering the world to benefit beings is truly not something small-faculty, inferior people can bear. After more than forty years of the work of teaching, he still spent such expedient spiritual power. Yet people today, living in the five turbidities, in the sea of affliction, birth, death and suffering, speak of emptiness with every mouth, talk of Chan and speak of the Way, and at every turn take the upward step as their own responsibility, despising the true Dharma, not fearing cause and effect, not knowing how to measure themselves — are they so wildly arrogant? Considering how our Buddha’s expedients and skillful means for benefiting beings cost him so much bitter effort, and how he did not dare lightly teach the single word of causing people to become Buddha, while people today casually speak of surpassing the Buddha and overleaping the patriarchs — if this is not absurd, what is? Should we not fear?

Only our Buddha, appearing in the world and teaching for forty-nine years, had the sutras collected into one great canon, and from beginning to end he spoke only eight words: “The three realms are mind only; the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only.” From the beginning until this point forty years had passed before he broke open the meaning of the single sentence “the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only”; and still he did not dare to reveal the purport of mind-only, because mind-only is the ultimate standard of all dharmas. From the first, the great disciples had already heard the gate of consciousness-only; therefore after this he taught the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, revealing the dharma gate that the three realms are mind only, wishing directly to cause people to awaken to this one mind and take it as the ultimate standard. If one gathers in the earlier two, emptiness and the provisional, extinguishes the two truths and returns altogether to the one mind, then one perfects the one mind, merges it into the middle way and makes principle complete. Hence the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says: “What is quiescent extinction is called the one mind; the one mind is called the Tathāgatagarbha.” It means that the storehouse of consciousness is the Tathāgatagarbha, neither empty nor existent. It points directly at the one mind, beyond names and cut off from marks, extinguishing sage and ordinary alike, not belonging to the stages of practice and realization. Suddenly contemplating the nature of the storehouse is called the realm of the wisdom of self-realization of the noble ones. One directly leaves all clinging and deluded mind; one need only understand that deluded thought has no nature, and one awakens to non-arising. This is the dharma gate of the sudden teaching. Bodhidharma, the patriarch, transmitted it to the Second Patriarch, Great Master Ke, taking this sutra as the mind-seal. Therefore this sutra is given solely to those of the very highest faculties, and the two vehicles have no share in it. In the patriarchs’ gate, therefore, beginners in Chan investigation must investigate apart from mind, intellect and consciousness, seek apart from the realm of deluded thought, and study beyond the paths of ordinary and sage. This sutra alone is taken as the summit. This teaching sets forth the ultimate standard of the one mind. After more than forty years, with much exposition from many sides and passing through how many dharma gates, only now was this sutra taught; and still the small faculties had no share in it. Yet monks and laypeople today, their eye of the teachings not yet clear and having no path of practice, are blind and unknowing; the deluded thoughts and clinging in their own minds — they do not know their arising and ceasing at all; day and night they never have a single thought of coolness. Yet they take the upward step of being apart from mind, intellect and consciousness as their own responsibility, without having dreamed of a huatou, and open their big mouths to talk of Chan. What must their self-deception be like? They may be called people of great shamelessness. Should we not fear? Moreover, today it is not only ignorant laypeople who talk wildly; even the monks who are later students in our Dharma gate, having never heard the Buddha’s dharma gate of cultivating the mind and wholly not knowing the work of applying the mind, merely entertain deluded thoughts for a while, with no right view at all, and then claim to have awakened to the Way and consider themselves sufficient. Whom then are they deceiving? Whom are they misleading? Be warned, be warned; be careful, be careful. Only after the Buddha had passed these forty years did he reveal the one-mind dharma gate; enough to show that the dharma is not easy to teach, not easy to practice, not easy to awaken to.

Only our Buddha, the World-Honored One, appeared in the world specially for the sake of one great matter. The one great matter is what is called the beings’ attainment of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Beings originally possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, but now they are deluded and take it as the knowledge and vision of deluded thought and birth and death. Through kalpas past they have been deluded without knowing it, like a poor son who holds a jewel yet begs, suffering hardship to no purpose. Therefore the Buddha aroused the great compassion of one substance and appeared in the world specially to open and demonstrate that beings originally possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and to cause them to awaken and enter it — like pointing out to the poor son the jewel sewn in his clothing, letting him know it himself and receive its use. Now the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is precisely the one mind spoken of in the Laṅkāvatāra, called the wisdom of self-realization of the noble ones. For a long time he did not dare teach it suddenly, because he saw that beings’ faculties were dull and they could not bear this dharma; so he long kept this essential matter silent and did not hasten to speak it. Only after forty years, having winnowed them in many ways, when their faculties were ripe and his teaching conditions were nearly at an end, did he teach the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, revealing the one-mind dharma gate as the completion of the revelation of principle. After that he immediately taught the Lotus Sūtra, revealing the true aspect of all dharmas as the completion of the revelation of affairs. This is the order of the Buddha’s teaching. Only when principle and affair are both complete is the ultimate standard of the one mind exhausted. Therefore the people of the two vehicles only at this point believed the Buddha’s mind decisively and without doubt, and awakened to the fact that each of them originally possessed the Buddha-nature and had never lost it. Like a poor son who has long fled to another country and now at last returns to see his father, they believed that the father’s estate was originally their own; mind and mark mutually trusting, they were fit to inherit the family estate, and so the elder entrusted it to them. It has been said that this one Lotus Sutra is like the elder’s testament entrusting the family estate; it is the Buddha’s ultimate original intent in benefiting beings. Therefore the Buddha gave each of his disciples a prediction that in the future they would certainly become Buddha, and said: “Of all who hear the Dharma, not one fails to become Buddha.” With this the one great matter’s causes and conditions were complete, and so it is the final teaching. Not long after this he entered nirvāṇa. Yet in the single assembly of the Lotus, our Buddha’s original intent in appearing in the world to benefit beings was already exhausted. As for the Nirvāṇa Sutra, it reveals the meaning of the Buddha-nature to gather in the faculties not yet complete from the Lotus and to break the doubts remaining in the earlier disciples. For the Buddha had said that of all who hear the Dharma, not one fails to become Buddha; and he feared that the disciples, having earlier heard that icchantikas, people without faith, were not permitted to become Buddha, might doubt this. Therefore this sutra says that icchantikas too have the Buddha-nature; hence the story of the broad-browed butcher who, putting down his cleaver, at once did the work of a Buddha. This makes it certain that all who have awareness will in the end become Buddha, decisively without doubt. Thus is the Tathāgata’s one appearance in the world, his ability to transform and benefit beings, brought to completion; and with this complete, he entered nirvāṇa. What has been said above is the whole ritual sequence of our Buddha’s appearing in the world and converting beings from first to last, the dharma gates of gradual cultivation of the cause. Though he saw that beings originally possess the Buddha-nature, each complete in full, and that none is unwilling to become Buddha, yet because the obstruction of affliction is thick and the roots of karmic offense are deep, they could not bear the sudden revelation of the great dharma; therefore the One Vehicle dharma was divided and taught as three. This is why the one vehicle and the three vehicles were established. Hence before the Laṅkāvatāra, the teaching was the expedient teaching of the three vehicles; the Laṅkāvatāra and the Lotus are the true teaching of the One Vehicle. Therefore the Tiantai school judged them as the teaching that opens the expedient and reveals the true. Thus we know that what was taught before the forty years had passed was all established as expedient, because faculties were unequal.

What has been said above, sudden and gradual, is not uniform, yet it is altogether the meaning of the teachings. Now the Laṅkāvatāra suddenly reveals the one mind as the Tathāgata’s pure Chan — and are the teachings then not the Chan school? As for the World-Honored One’s own words, “In forty-nine years I have not spoken a single word,” and at the very end his holding up a flower before the assembly: of the millions of gods and humans, all were bewildered and did not know, and only Kāśyapa alone broke into a smile.

The World-Honored One then said: “I have the treasury of the right Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa; I entrust it to you.” This is the purport of the special transmission outside the teachings. From there it was transmitted second to Ānanda, and so on to the twenty-eight patriarchs of India and the six of China, until Bodhidharma came from the West, and it was regarded as the Chan school: not establishing words and letters, pointing directly at the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming Buddha — called the single-transmission dharma gate. Hence from Caoxi onward, the two schools and five houses, and the seventeen hundred people recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp, were all great beings who had awakened the mind. Whatever sayings they had were called koans, because Chan is originally beyond words; only this phrase or half-phrase is kept as evidence of the mind-seal, like the case files of a public court. It is not that people should take these as fixed dharmas, spreading them by mouth and ear and taking them as their own profound and wondrous views. Now our Buddha had already taught a whole great canon; as for the one-mind dharma gate, what does it not contain? Yet he must make the holding up of the flower the heart-essence, because the purport of the one mind is beyond the mark of speech, beyond the mark of names, beyond the mark of mental activity. Though those who heard before had awakened to the original mind, some could not yet leave marks behind; so the holding up of the flower at the end was a device to dispel the habit of clinging to words, to cure the disease of clinging to names and phrases — a golden lancet, as it were. People today do not know that the teachings and Chan are the purport of one mind, and that both are our Buddha’s expedients for converting beings. Each person wildly grasps one side and takes it as the necessary truth: thus those who grasp the teachings reject Chan, and those who grasp Chan reject the teachings. Those who grasp the teachings and reject Chan have indeed misled themselves; but those who grasp Chan and reject the teachings mislead themselves still more. For one who grasps Chan clings to his own folly and takes himself as right, wildly accepting his own views, and so misleads himself, denouncing the Mahāyāna sutras of definitive meaning as mere words, until in the end he accomplishes nothing. Still more pitiable: observe this age of the Dharma’s end — the lecture halls have declined and there are no great master craftsmen; clever young men lack the wisdom of much hearing, and even those who aspire to investigate Chan upward have no firm and lasting resolve. Lacking a clear-eyed teacher, they merely follow their feelings and cheat and delude, so that many fall by the way. This is enough to make one weep. Moreover there are monks who wildly think themselves awakened, deceiving the ignorant worldlings and greedily seeking offerings. When someone takes refuge with them, they immediately instruct him in Chan investigation as the upward step; and when the believer’s huatou is not yet ripe, his deluded thoughts seething in all directions, they at once seal and confirm him, saying he has awakened in eight places, so that he falls into wrong views. Such harm is even greater. This above all one must know to fear and examine oneself. In my humble view, it is not that Chan investigation is not wanted, but that people investigate without truth and lack a firm and lasting resolve, wildly taking themselves as awakened and misleading many. In my humble opinion, whether one reads the teachings without being able to investigate Chan, or investigates Chan without resolve, it is always better to devote oneself single-mindedly to the Pure Land work and at least not waste this life. The wise will judge for themselves. Let each reflect; I hope you will not deceive and mislead yourselves.

I have observed that among officials and scholars there have been no few from ancient times who investigated Chan and awakened, as the records of the Transmission of the Lamp clearly show — not one man alone. Among officials of this age, those who aspire to protect the Dharma gate from outside mostly take Chan investigation as the upward path. This is not to be judged by the common measure; there is surely a reason. For in the past there were men of the Dharma gate who practiced Chan and, before fully awakening, vowed to protect and uphold the Buddhadharma; there were also patriarchs with great vows to save beings, and bodhisattvas manifesting to rescue the world; and there were also those who formerly, as monks, investigated without penetrating and then, drawn by habitual karma, now appear in the world. Though they are amid the dusty toil of conventional truth, the seed of prajñā from a single thought of past habit shines forth and cannot be hidden, and so it issues as literary works, rank and achievement, and they become outer protectors of the Dharma gate. Their expedients and functions differ, and their practices are not of one kind. Some devote themselves to the upward path; some to meritorious practice; some to establishing the Three Jewels, fulfilling vows and protecting the Dharma; some solely for their own birth and death; some to express loyalty and filial piety. All their various practices are bodhisattva paths; they cannot be judged uniformly by the practices of monks. Among monks, too, not all know the two schools of Chan and the teachings: there are ascetic dhuta practitioners; there are those devoted to the Pure Land work; there are those of true practice; there are those who follow conditions in Buddhist affairs to help propagate the Dharma; and there are those who recite and copy scriptures as their practice. All these are within the Buddha’s white-hair light, seeking the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions, and cannot be judged by one measure. Therefore among officials, whoever has the deep heart of protecting the Dharma need only take up one practice of the monks, and that is enough; there is no need for every one of them to investigate Chan to be practicing rightly. Now Chan investigation, though wondrous, is in truth not within the capacity of small faculties. In the Buddha’s time, of the millions of gods and humans, only Kāśyapa alone received the transmission; Bodhidharma came from the West and got only the Second Patriarch; of the seven hundred at Huangmei, only the Sixth Patriarch sealed the mind. Is this a small matter? If among monks there is but one practice that can serve the true business of the Dharma gate and can teach and convert beings, that is a bodhisattva. Hence it is said: all the various practices are bodhisattva paths. If one thing in a man is worth taking, then no man is to be cast aside; if one seeks what is lacking in a good man, then no man is whole. From ancient times, in the world and beyond it, a whole man is hard to find. All this tangle of words, down to the sequence of the Buddha’s rituals for converting beings — did the Buddha not want people to awaken suddenly to their own minds and become Buddha on the spot? But beings’ faculties are dull, and he could not but use expedients to draw them in. The ancients said: “If a monk cannot awaken to his own mind, let him at least set his heart on the teachings; then his time is not wasted.” I would say that monks today, even if they cannot investigate Chan or read the teachings, if they can keep the precepts, recite sutras, create merit and protect the Dharma, are still ten thousand times better than the ordinary brood of demons. Among lay believers, whoever can keep the fast, recite the Buddha’s name and help propagate the Three Jewels is practicing truly. This is what all Buddhas hope for. I beg the wise and accomplished gentlemen of every quarter to trust this themselves, and be careful not to take my foolish words as absurd.

inline.s: Instruction to the Practitioners of Yihua

In the winter of the guichou year the old man came from eastern Guangdong with staff in hand to Mount Nan, and passing through Yizhang was met by the good man Kuang Shaozhen and more than twenty others, who welcomed him in the sutra hall, bowed reverently and made offerings, and requested instruction. He briefly spoke the essentials of the Dharma and departed after one night. Afterwards the old man stayed in hiding at the Linghu hermitage, where he established recitation services.

The Avataṃsaka assembly. In the sixth month of the summer of the yimao year, Shaozhen and the others came from afar to pay their respects, arriving just as the old man was expounding the Diamond Prajñā for the assembly. Hearing it with joy, they were filled with great delight, offered incense and asked for instruction on the essentials of practice for laypeople. The old man accordingly instructed them, saying: “Yizhang lies in deep mountains and a remote region, where no good teacher passes through; though there are many faithful laypeople, they have not heard the true Dharma. Now all of you should each keep the five precepts diligently as your right practice. These five precepts were taught by our Buddha especially for lay good men; they are the five constants of the Confucian school: benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom and trustworthiness. Hence it is said: ‘If the five precepts are not kept, the road to gods and humans is cut off.’ Therefore lay good men should uphold them. Having kept the five precepts, do not listen to or believe heterodox teachers and teachings that wildly speak of the emptiness of dharmas, deny cause and effect, cut off the Buddha-seed and create the karma of hell. You should only rely wholly on the Buddha’s teaching, devote yourselves single-mindedly to the Western Pure Land dharma gate, and take Buddha-recitation as your right practice. Now the Pure Land gate draws in beings and benefits them most widely; from ancient times to now very many who recited the Buddha’s name have attained rebirth there. But single-mindedness and diligence are the main thing; it is not a matter of one or two gatherings a month and reciting a few thousand Buddha-names — that is not to be taken as right practice. First of all, you must arouse your minds and deeply weary of Sahā as suffering, resolve to forsake it, and keep the Western Pure Land in mind — lotus-born by transformation. Thought after thought you must be determined to be reborn in that land and see Amitābha face to face, taking this as your original vow. Every day, morning and evening, you must set fixed lessons: whether holding the Diamond Sutra, the Amitābha Sutra or the Rebirth Mantra, you must recite the Buddha’s name and dedicate the merit toward the West, vowing to be reborn there. Make this your settled rule. Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, whether at leisure or busy, moving or still, hold the single recitation ‘Amitābha Buddha’ in your mind, never forgetting it thought after thought, never letting it break, so that even in sleep and dreams you do not lose it. Thus beating it into one piece without interruption is called the samādhi of one practice. When this recitation is ripe, no condition can interrupt it: eyes open or closed, the single recitation ‘Amitābha Buddha’ stands clearly before you, and all the world’s parents, wives and children, all kinds of affectionate deluded thoughts and karmic notions, are ground away and purified by the one Buddha-name. Thus you attain the purity of your own mind. The sutra says: ‘When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.’ Reciting the Buddha’s name in this way and applying the mind in this way, when you come to the end of life there will be only the single recitation ‘Amitābha Buddha’ present before you, with a mind undistracted; you will naturally see Amitābha Buddha come in person to welcome you, and in the space of a single thought be reborn in the Pure Land. From then on you will forever escape the suffering of birth and death, rise to the Land of Ultimate Bliss and be born by transformation in a lotus — this is the proof of a lifetime of Buddha-recitation. If one is thus single-minded and devoted and still is not reborn, then all the Buddhas would be guilty of false speech. But if the years drift idly by while the mouth speaks of Buddha-recitation and the mind has no true practice, that is deceiving and cheating oneself; when would there ever be a time of proof? Good men, since you have aroused faith, you should practice truly. Above all, do not deceive yourselves.”
